title: Why is NASA bringing 7,500 contractors back to work as civil servants?
gist: NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman is converting 7,500 contractor positions into civil servants to rebuild in-house 'core competencies,' claiming $100M+ in early savings potentially rising to over $1B; contractors Armentum, Jacobs and KBR dispute the savings and warn of lost flexibility, but NASA's safety panel endorsed the move.

insights.claim: NASA is converting 7,500 contract positions into civil servant roles as part of Isaacman's 'workforce initiative' to rebuild core competencies, a largely under-the-radar but massive shift in how the agency operates.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: A structural reduction in NASA's outsourced engineering services spend.
insights.quote: Isaacman is bringing 7,500 contract positions back into the agency, making them civil servants
insights.locator: This year, in a move that has largely

insights.claim: Isaacman says early pilots identified more than $100 million in savings from converting contractors, potentially growing to over $1 billion, citing layered management, third-party tools and contractual barriers in contractor structures.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: If savings materialize, the model could spread to other agencies reliant on services contractors.
insights.quote: early pilots of the workforce initiative had already identified more than $100 million in savings
insights.locator: Isaacman has said NASA will benefit

insights.claim: Contracting firms dispute NASA's savings claims, saying their overhead is only about 2-3 percent of an employee's compensation.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: The true savings are contested; investors should treat the $1B figure skeptically.
insights.quote: the overhead they charge is only about 2 or 3 percent of an employee’s compensation.

insights.claim: Armentum, Jacobs Engineering Group and KBR are the most affected contractors, each having provided a few thousand contractors to NASA field centers.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Direct revenue headwind for these government-services firms' NASA business lines.
insights.quote: The largest and most directly affected contractors are Armentum, Jacobs Engineering Group, and KBR.
insights.locator: The largest and most directly affected

insights.claim: Before the initiative NASA had about 40,000 contractors and 14,000 civil servants (down ~4,000 from early 2025 after DOGE programs); it now has about 21,000 civil servants, more than before the second Trump administration began.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: NASA is growing federal headcount counter to the administration-wide reduction push.
insights.quote: NASA has a considerably larger civil servant workforce today than before the outset of the second Trump administration—about 21,000 people.
insights.locator: But this is not really an effort

insights.claim: Apollo flight director Gerry Griffin argues that Mission Control positions should be held by NASA employees because the agency bears ultimate responsibility for mission success, and that outsourcing of those roles grew midway through the shuttle era.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Frames insourcing as restoring accountability rather than ideology.
insights.quote: Midway through the space shuttle era, I was surprised to find that a lot of the jobs in Mission Control had gone to contractors
insights.locator: After he left NASA, that began to change.

insights.claim: Critical jobs were often outsourced historically as a way to increase NASA headcount without raising the civil service count.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Contractor reliance was partly an accounting workaround on federal headcount limits.
insights.quote: often as a way to increase headcount at the space agency without raising the NASA civil service count, critical jobs were outsourced
insights.locator: Griffin doesn’t want to denigrate contractors.

insights.claim: During Artemis II, NASA launch controllers lacked direct access to ground-system schematics due to contractor IP rules and had to view them via Microsoft Teams screen sharing, illustrating the barriers insourcing aims to remove.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Contractor IP ownership can impair operational control in critical moments, a driver for insourcing.
insights.quote: You would be sitting there with some tool that’s livestreaming someone else’s display, trying to see a schematic
insights.locator: When there was an issue on the launch pad

insights.claim: Industry critics argue the contractor system gave NASA flexibility to change direction by not renewing contracts, which is lost with civil servants who have stronger job protections.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Insourcing converts variable costs into sticky fixed costs, reducing future program agility.
insights.quote: if the agency decided to change directions, it could simply not renew a contract with a contractor.
insights.locator: Beyond the frustrations of some individual

insights.claim: Some industry officials believe losing the contractor ecosystem will weaken NASA's lobbying support in Congress, making funding harder to secure and some programs more vulnerable.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: A second-order political cost: fewer private stakeholders advocating for NASA budgets.
insights.quote: if this contractor support goes away, NASA’s efforts to secure Congressional funding may be more difficult
insights.locator: This contractor ecosystem also supports NASA

insights.claim: The author views Isaacman's ability to grow the federal workforce while the White House pushes for cuts as evidence of his political skill and intent to build NASA rather than shrink it.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Signals NASA has unusual political latitude under current leadership.
insights.quote: it reflects Isaacman’s political skill that he was able to increase the federal workforce at a time when the White House has been pushing for reductions.

insights.claim: NASA's independent Aerospace Safety Advisory Panel, often critical of the agency, endorsed the workforce conversion as 'a coherent and necessary vision' and found no critical concerns despite challenges from its speed and scope.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Undercuts critics' claims that the transition will delay Artemis or raise safety risk.
insights.quote: the administrator’s directive is a coherent and necessary vision for the future of NASA’s workforce.
